documents.title: Market data and risk factor time series documentation

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the market data and risk factor time series data set (RFTS) that serves the Market Risk – Expected Shortfall model (inventory identifier MDL-13, model version 3.0) under the alternative internal model approach (IMA) of CRR Part Three, Title IV, Chapter 1b. The RFTS covers all risk factors of positions held on the five trading desks proposed for the IMA: D01 EUR Rates Linear, D02 Rates Options, D03 G10 FX, D04 Credit Flow and D05 Covered Bonds and SSA, booked in Amsterdam and in the London branch. It is used to calibrate the current and stressed partial expected shortfall (ES) measures, the stress scenario risk measure (SSRM) for non-modellable risk factors, the back-testing VaR and the risk-theoretical P&L, and it supplies the credit spread and equity histories and issuer default probabilities used by the default risk charge (DRC). The document follows the RDS documentation template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A; where a template section addresses credit default data that has no counterpart in market data, the heading is retained with the statement "Not applicable" and a justification. The frozen data set referenced throughout is RFTS-2026Q4-F1, which is also referenced in chapter 3 of the ES model documentation (EVD-13-MDD).

sections.heading: Governance and ownership of market data
sections.text: Each data domain from which the RFTS is sourced has exactly one Data Owner recorded in the Group Data Catalogue: Market Data (Head of Market Data Services), Trading Positions and Valuations (Head of Product Control), Instrument and Issuer Reference Data (Head of Reference Data) and Credit Risk Parameters (Head of Credit Risk Modelling) for the IRB PDs used in the DRC. The model owner agreed the data quality expectations for the critical data elements with these four Data Owners in data quality agreement DQA-MR-2026-04 of 14 October 2026. Roles for the ownership and quality of risk data are defined for the business (Data Owners and Data Stewards in Market Data Services and Product Control) and for IT (the Risk Data Platform team, which operates the Market Data Repository and the RFTS build). The risk data aggregation for the IMA runs on the Risk Data Platform, whose governance framework was approved by the Management Board within the Bank's BCBS 239 programme and is consistent with DATA-POL-001 and MRM-POL-001. Changes to the definition, source or transformation of an RFTS data element are approved by the Data Owner and announced to the model owner at least one monthly calibration cycle in advance through the data change request (DCR) process. Data quality is managed under MRM-STD-022, as documented in the data quality report EVD-13-DQ.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RFTS contains daily (TARGET business day) level observations from 1 December 2006 to 31 December 2026, 5,140 business days, so that ten-day returns are available for every business day of the stress period search window 1 January 2007 to 31 December 2026. It contains 14,812 risk factors (interest rate 3,964; credit spread 8,236; foreign exchange 2,612); the reduced set of 2,146 risk factors has full history over the entire period, while the remaining 12,666 risk factors are required only for the current 12-month window of 256 business days (2 January 2026 to 31 December 2026). In total the frozen data set holds 14,272,936 risk factor observations. As the model has no default-based target, the number of target events is replaced by the number of daily P&L observations used for back-testing and the P&L attribution (PLA) test: 250 business days of hypothetical and actual P&L per IMA desk for 2026, 1,250 desk-days in total. The IMA desks held no equity or commodity positions at the reference date; the corresponding broad risk factor categories are therefore empty.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts before the global financial crisis and ends at the RDS reference date of 31 December 2026. It contains the 2008–2009 financial crisis, the euro area sovereign debt crisis of 2010–2012, the period of negative euro interest rates from 2014 to 2022, the COVID-19 market turmoil of March 2020, the interest rate shock of 2022 and the banking stress of March 2023, and therefore covers the full range of stress conditions relevant to rates, credit spread and FX positions. The stress period is identified over this window as the continuous 12-month period that maximises the ES of the current portfolio calculated with the reduced set of risk factors, as required by Article 325bc(2)(c) CRR and MR-STD-500 §5.3. In 2014 the Market Data Repository (MDR) replaced the legacy RiskStore database; the history before 2014 was migrated and reconciled point by point, and the 0.02% of observations that differed by more than one basis point were corrected from the original vendor files. The migration is recorded in the lineage (Annex A) so that the consistency of the time series over the observation period can be traced.

sections.heading: Current calibration window and update frequency
sections.text: Data inputs for the current partial ES measures are calibrated to the preceding 12 months; the window rolls forward daily, appending the latest business day and dropping the oldest, which exceeds the minimum monthly update frequency of Article 325bc(3)(c) CRR. The stressed window is fixed between quarterly stress period reviews, and the reduced-set time series are extended daily so that a review can be performed at any time. End-of-day market data for business day T are available in the MDR by 06:30 CET on T+1, the RFTS increment is built by 07:15 CET and the ES, SSRM and back-testing runs complete by 09:30 CET, which meets the daily reporting deadline of 10:00 CET in normal times and was maintained during the March 2023 stress with an intraday rerun. A monthly snapshot of the rolling data set is frozen on the second business day of each month for reproducibility of production results.

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The ES model has no default-based target; its outcome variables are the daily P&L measures used for back-testing and the PLA test, with a one-business-day outcome horizon, while ES itself uses a ten-day base horizon. Hypothetical P&L (HPL) is the difference between the end-of-day value of the desk portfolio on business day t and its value on t+1 assuming unchanged positions, revalued with the front-office pricing models; actual P&L (APL) compares the end-of-day value on t with the actual value on t+1 and excludes fees and commissions as well as valuation adjustments subject to a separate capital treatment or deducted from CET1. Risk-theoretical P&L (RTPL) is the daily P&L of the same positions produced by the ES engine using only the risk factors of the risk-measurement model. HPL and APL are sourced per desk and business day from the PnL Hub of Product Control; RTPL is produced by the ES engine. HPL, APL and RTPL are designated critical data elements, together with every reduced-set risk factor time series, the RFET observation counts and the position sensitivities used for the PLA risk factor analysis.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: Not applicable. The ES model does not use a default-based target variable, and the DRC uses issuer default probabilities rather than default flags constructed from the Bank's own obligor data. No deviation from the definition of default in CR-STD-110 therefore arises in the RFTS. Where the DRC uses an IRB PD, that PD is based on the Bank's prudential definition of default through the rating system of record; where it uses an external PD, the rating agency default definition applies, as explained in section 3.3.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: The ES component has no default definition; this section documents the default data used by the DRC. Where an IRB PD exists for the issuer (1,146 of the 1,882 DRC issuers at 31 December 2026), the PD of the rating system of record is taken from the Credit Rating System, and the source of each PD (IRB model identifier or external mapping) is stored in the field PD_SOURCE; all PDs are floored at 0.03%, or at 0.01% for exposures eligible for a 0% risk weight and covered bonds eligible for a 10% risk weight. For the other issuers, default probabilities are derived from the S&P Global Ratings and Moody's annual default studies for corporates and sovereigns covering 1981–2025, i.e. considerably more than five years of historical default data, mapped to the Bank's master scale; they are not inferred from current market prices. The prudential definition of default of CR-STD-110 underlying the IRB PDs and the rating agency definition underlying the external PDs are labelled distinctly (DEF_PRUD and DEF_AGENCY) in the Group Data Catalogue, and the difference is documented in Annex A.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: Not applicable. The RFTS does not construct default flags and therefore does not use unlikeliness-to-pay triggers. Issuer defaults relevant to the DRC are captured through the PD sources described in section 3.3, and realised issuer defaults of trading book positions are recorded by Product Control in the PnL Hub as jump-to-default P&L, which enters APL and HPL. No expert labelling of target events takes place, so no labelling guidelines are required for this data set.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RFTS draws on four source categories: front-office positions and valuations (trading system Apex and the PnL Hub), external market data received through the MDR, instrument and issuer reference data (RefHub) and IRB PDs from the Credit Rating System (CRS). An authoritative source is defined for every data type: the MDR for end-of-day market data (official close at 17:30 CET), Apex for positions, the PnL Hub for HPL and APL, RefHub for issuer and instrument static data and the CRS for IRB PDs. Lineage from each source system to the RFTS and onwards to the production input data of the ES engine is documented for every variable in Annex A, including discarded raw fields such as bid and ask quotes used to derive mid prices. The data are mapped to the four data domains named in section 1.2 in the same annex. The lineage allows every risk factor observation and every P&L figure to be traced from the vendor delivery or source system to the ES report. Instruments, issuers and legal entities are identified with the Group identifiers (ISIN, LEI and internal issuer ID), and risk factors follow the Group naming convention RF-<class>-<currency>-<curve>-<tenor> maintained in the Group Data Catalogue.

sections.heading: Front-office position and valuation data
sections.text: Positions are extracted from Apex at the official end-of-day snapshot of 17:30 CET; at 31 December 2026 the five IMA desks held 41,620 positions with a gross absolute market value of EUR 24.6 billion. Each trading book position is booked in exactly one Apex book and each book is assigned to exactly one trading desk of the approved desk structure; the build rejects any position whose book has no or more than one desk assignment, which did not occur in 2026. For each variable the lineage identifies the source fields, the Risk Data Platform staging tables, every transformation, filter, join and aggregation with a reference to the ETL job (for example rdp_pos_eod_v4 and rfts_sens_agg_v2), and the extraction frequency and timing (daily at 18:15 CET). Positions and sensitivities cover both legal booking locations, Amsterdam and the London branch, and all asset types of the IMA desks.

sections.heading: External market data vendors
sections.text: End-of-day market data are received from four vendors: Bloomberg (government bond and swap rates, FX spot and forwards, BVAL bond prices), LSEG (broker quotes for swaption, cap and floor and FX option volatilities), S&P Global Market Intelligence (single-name and index CDS curves) and ICE Data Services (corporate and covered bond prices). For each vendor feed the lineage starts at the point of receipt in the MDR landing zone and records the provider, the data product (for example S&P Global CDS Pricing End-of-Day or Bloomberg BVAL Corporate) and the delivery date and file version. Each vendor delivery is subject to file-count and record-count checks on receipt, and critical series are compared daily with a secondary vendor (section 6.3). Vendor contracts and service levels are managed by Market Data Services under TPR-POL-001.

sections.heading: Real price observations for the RFET
sections.text: The modellability of every risk factor of positions on the IMA desks is assessed as of each quarter end on the real price observations of the preceding twelve months, taken from the Bank's own executed transactions in Apex, committed quotes captured from electronic trading venues and one third-party observation pooling vendor. Observations from the vendor were presented to the ECB in the pre-application meeting of 9 December 2026 and will be used for the own funds requirements only to the extent permitted in the IMA decision; until then the RFET is also run without vendor observations and both results are reported. The use of the vendor is documented together with its controls: daily completeness checks on the observation file, a quarterly verification of a sample of 200 observations traced by the vendor to trade confirmations, and a review of the vendor's annual ISAE 3402 assurance report. At the Q4 2026 assessment, 14,431 risk factors were modellable and 381 were non-modellable (interest rate 46, credit spread 297, FX 38).

sections.heading: Lineage to the ES engine
sections.text: The data flow runs from the MDR and Apex through the RFTS build (Python and PySpark, repository mr-rfts-build) into the read-only RFTS store and from there into the ES engine input tables. The lineage of the development data (RFTS-2026Q4-F1) and of the production input data of the ES engine was compared at implementation: both are produced by the same build code and differ only in refresh timing (monthly frozen snapshot versus daily increment), which has no effect on model outputs, as confirmed by the reconciliation in EVD-13-IMPL section 5. Aggregation is fully automated except for the manual interventions listed in section 4.6.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Of the 19,966 candidate series in the MDR, the following were excluded from the RFTS, stated with number and share of candidate series: (a) risk factors used only by the non-IMA desks D06 Equity Derivatives and D07 Emerging Markets Rates and FX, 3,420 series (17.1%); (b) risk factors to which no IMA position had sensitivity at the reference date, 1,108 series (5.5%); (c) discontinued benchmark curves after their cessation dates (EONIA, EUR, GBP, CHF and JPY LIBOR, USD LIBOR), 214 series (1.1%); and (d) duplicate vendor series for the same risk factor, 412 series (2.1%). Because the target events of this data set are desk P&L observations, the default count per exclusion is not applicable; no P&L observation of an IMA desk was excluded. No exclusion affects positions of the IMA desks, so the excluded share of exposure is 0% and the approval threshold of 5% in MRM-STD-022 §5.3 is not reached; the impact analysis in section 5.3 concludes that the exclusions have no effect on ES. Excluded series remain in the MDR and are re-included automatically when an IMA position acquires sensitivity to them.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are classified per risk factor as missing for a structural reason (local market holidays, instruments not yet in existence), missing at random (vendor delivery failures on individual days) or missing because of a data deficiency (for example discontinued vendor coverage), and are recorded with a reason code in the field FILL_REASON. Gaps of up to five consecutive business days are filled by linear interpolation of the level between the adjacent observations; the method is implemented in the build code and therefore reproducible, the share of filled points is reported per risk factor category in Annex C (0.41% of reduced-set observations in the current window and 2.6% in the stress period), and the effect on ES is assessed quarterly (−0.3% on the stressed reduced-set ES at the Q4 2026 review). Gaps longer than five business days are closed with proxies (section 4.4). Outliers are identified with a documented criterion, a daily return exceeding six times the robust standard deviation (1.4826 times the median absolute deviation over the preceding 250 business days), which is applied identically in the production data controls. Flagged returns are investigated by Market Data Services against a second vendor: confirmed market moves are retained unchanged (1,211 of 1,284 flags over the observation period, including the removal of the EUR/CHF floor on 15 January 2015), while 73 erroneous observations were replaced by the secondary vendor value, with a quantified impact on the stressed reduced-set ES of +0.1%.

sections.heading: Risk factor taxonomy and liquidity horizon mapping
sections.text: Every risk factor in the RFTS carries exactly one broad risk factor category and one broad risk factor sub-category of Table 2 of Article 325bd CRR in the fields RF_CAT and RF_SUBCAT, from which its liquidity horizon of 10, 20, 40, 60 or 120 days is derived. Interest rate risk factors in EUR (the domestic currency) and in the most liquid currencies are mapped to 10 days, other currencies to 20 days and interest rate volatilities to 60 days; sovereign and SSA credit spreads rated investment grade are mapped to 20 days, covered bond and other corporate investment grade credit spreads to 40 days, high yield corporate credit spreads to 60 days and credit spread volatilities to 120 days; the most liquid FX pairs are mapped to 10 days, other pairs to 20 days and FX volatilities to 40 days. The appropriateness of the mapping is verified monthly through an automated check of all new risk factors and a review of changes in currency liquidity classification and issuer ratings, with the results recorded in the monthly liquidity horizon attestation (latest attestation 8 January 2027). The mapping table itself is documented in Annex A and in EVD-13-MDD section 4.2.1.

sections.heading: Manual interventions

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: For a market data set, representativeness means that the risk factors capture the risks of the current portfolio and that the stress-period data represent the current portfolio's behaviour in stress. At 31 December 2026 the modelled risk factors capture 99.2% of the front-office interest rate delta (PV01), 98.1% of the credit spread sensitivity (CS01) and 97.4% of the vega of the IMA desks; the uncaptured remainder relates to basis and smile risk factors recorded in the RNIME inventory (EVD-13-MDD section 8.3). The reduced set explains on average 86% of the current full-set ES over the 60 business days to 31 December 2026, which confirms that the stress-period calibration is representative of the current risk profile. The PLA test results for Q4 2026 (four desks green, one amber) provide further evidence that the risk factor set is representative of the desks' front-office valuations. Detailed tables per desk and sensitivity type are presented in Annex B.

sections.heading: Time series quality checks
sections.text: For every risk factor time series the build computes the number of filled data points, the number of replaced data points, the number of days without a daily change and the maximum number of consecutive days without a change; series with more than 10% unchanged days, or a run of more than ten consecutive unchanged days, in the current window are flagged as stale. In the current window 146 series were flagged stale, mainly long-dated CDS tenors and illiquid covered bond curves; all were reviewed, and 131 of them are also non-modellable under the RFET. Timeliness is measured as the lag between the close and availability in the MDR: data were available by 07:00 CET on 253 of 256 business days in 2026, and the three late days (vendor delays) were within the red threshold. Consistency is assessed between the RFTS and the production input data (identical by construction), over the observation period (including the benchmark rate transition) and as logical consistency between related fields, such as monotonic discount factors and arbitrage-free volatility surfaces.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the market data and risk factor time series data set (RFTS) that serves the Market Risk – Expected Shortfall model (inventory identifier MDL-13, model version 3.0) under the alternative internal model approach (IMA) of CRR Part Three, Title IV, Chapter 1b. The RFTS covers all risk factors of positions held on the five trading desks proposed for the IMA: D01 EUR Rates Linear, D02 Rates Options, D03 G10 FX, D04 Credit Flow and D05 Covered Bonds and SSA, booked in Amsterdam and in the London branch. It is used to calibrate the current and stressed partial expected shortfall (ES) measures, the stress scenario risk measure (SSRM) for non-modellable risk factors, the back-testing VaR and the risk-theoretical P&L, and it supplies the credit spread and equity histories and issuer default probabilities used by the default risk charge (DRC). The document follows the RDS documentation template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A; where a template section addresses credit default data that has no counterpart in market data, the heading is retained with the statement "Not applicable" and a justification. The frozen data set referenced throughout is RFTS-2026Q4-F1, which is also referenced in chapter 3 of the ES model documentation (EVD-13-MDD).

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The window starts before the global financial crisis and ends at the RDS reference date of 31 December 2026. It contains the 2008–2009 financial crisis, the euro area sovereign debt crisis of 2010–2012, the period of negative euro interest rates from 2014 to 2022, the COVID-19 market turmoil of March 2020, the interest rate shock of 2022 and the banking stress of March 2023, and therefore covers the full range of stress conditions relevant to rates, credit spread and FX positions. The stress period is identified over this window as the continuous 12-month period that maximises the ES of the current portfolio calculated with the reduced set of risk factors, as required by Article 325bc(2)(c) CRR and MR-STD-500 §5.3. In 2014 the Market Data Repository (MDR) replaced the legacy RiskStore database; the history before 2014 was migrated and reconciled point by point, and the 0.02% of observations that differed by more than one basis point were corrected from the original vendor files. The migration is recorded in the lineage (Annex A) so that the consistency of the time series over the observation period can be traced.

sections.heading: Current calibration window and update frequency
sections.text: Data inputs for the current partial ES measures are calibrated to the preceding 12 months; the window rolls forward daily, appending the latest business day and dropping the oldest, which exceeds the minimum monthly update frequency of Article 325bc(3)(c) CRR. The stressed window is fixed between quarterly stress period reviews, and the reduced-set time series are extended daily so that a review can be performed at any time. End-of-day market data for business day T are available in the MDR by 06:30 CET on T+1, the RFTS increment is built by 07:15 CET and the ES, SSRM and back-testing runs complete by 09:30 CET, which meets the daily reporting deadline of 10:00 CET in normal times and was maintained during the March 2023 stress with an intraday rerun. sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The ES model has no default-based target; its outcome variables are the daily P&L measures used for back-testing and the PLA test, with a one-business-day outcome horizon, while ES itself uses a ten-day base horizon. Hypothetical P&L (HPL) is the difference between the end-of-day value of the desk portfolio on business day t and its value on t+1 assuming unchanged positions, revalued with the front-office pricing models; actual P&L (APL) compares the end-of-day value on t with the actual value on t+1 and excludes fees and commissions as well as valuation adjustments subject to a separate capital treatment or deducted from CET1. Risk-theoretical P&L (RTPL) is the daily P&L of the same positions produced by the ES engine using only the risk factors of the risk-measurement model. HPL and APL are sourced per desk and business day from the PnL Hub of Product Control; RTPL is produced by the ES engine. HPL, APL and RTPL are designated critical data elements, together with every reduced-set risk factor time series, the RFET observation counts and the position sensitivities used for the PLA risk factor analysis.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: Not applicable. The ES model does not use a default-based target variable, and the DRC uses issuer default probabilities rather than default flags constructed from the Bank's own obligor data. sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: The ES component has no default definition; this section documents the default data used by the DRC. Where an IRB PD exists for the issuer (1,146 of the 1,882 DRC issuers at 31 December 2026), the PD of the rating system of record is taken from the Credit Rating System, and the source of each PD (IRB model identifier or external mapping) is stored in the field PD_SOURCE; all PDs are floored at 0.03%, or at 0.01% for exposures eligible for a 0% risk weight and covered bonds eligible for a 10% risk weight. sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are classified per risk factor as missing for a structural reason (local market holidays, instruments not yet in existence), missing at random (vendor delivery failures on individual days) or missing because of a data deficiency (for example discontinued vendor coverage), and are recorded with a reason code in the field FILL_REASON. Gaps of up to five consecutive business days are filled by linear interpolation of the level between the adjacent observations; the method is implemented in the build code and therefore reproducible, the share of filled points is reported per risk factor category in Annex C (0.41% of reduced-set observations in the current window and 2.6% in the stress period), and the effect on ES is assessed quarterly (−0.3% on the stressed reduced-set ES at the Q4 2026 review). Gaps longer than five business days are closed with proxies (section 4.4). Outliers are identified with a documented criterion, a daily return exceeding six times the robust standard deviation (1.4826 times the median absolute deviation over the preceding 250 business days), which is applied identically in the production data controls. Flagged returns are investigated by Market Data Services against a second vendor: confirmed market moves are retained unchanged (1,211 of 1,284 flags over the observation period, including the removal of the EUR/CHF floor on 15 January 2015), while 73 erroneous observations were replaced by the secondary vendor value, with a quantified impact on the stressed reduced-set ES of +0.1%.

sections.heading: Proxies and data filling
sections.text: Proxies are used only where the history of a risk factor is insufficient, mainly in the stress period, and are selected for a demonstrated track record for the actual position and calibrated conservatively: for 318 of the 2,146 reduced-set risk factors (14.8%) the stress-period history is proxied, of which 204 single-name CDS curves by sector and rating iTraxx or CDX sub-index curves scaled with a beta estimated over the available history and floored at 1.0, 61 risk-free rate curve points by their predecessor rates (€STR before 1 October 2019 as EONIA minus 8.5 basis points), and 53 covered bond spread curves by the iBoxx EUR Covered index spread of the corresponding rating and tenor. The track record of each proxy is tested quarterly on the period in which both proxy and actual history exist; a proxy is accepted if the correlation of daily returns exceeds 0.70 and the ratio of the 97.5% ES of proxy returns to actual returns is at least 0.90. The impact of all proxies on ES is quantified quarterly by replacing each proxy with the next alternative in the proxy hierarchy; at the Q4 2026 review the proxies increased the stressed reduced-set ES by 2.3% compared with the alternatives. The proxy hierarchy and the beta floor are expert judgements recorded as EJ-13-04 and EJ-13-05 in the expert judgement log (EVD-13-MDD chapter 11), approved by the model owner and the Head of Market & Treasury Risk Modelling after challenge by Model Validation. Both judgements address data deficiencies DD-13-01 and DD-13-02 and are cross-referenced to them in section 6.2.

sections.heading: Risk factor taxonomy and liquidity horizon mapping
sections.text: Every risk factor in the RFTS carries exactly one broad risk factor category and one broad risk factor sub-category of Table 2 of Article 325bd CRR in the fields RF_CAT and RF_SUBCAT, from which its liquidity horizon of 10, 20, 40, 60 or 120 days is derived. Interest rate risk factors in EUR (the domestic currency) and in the most liquid currencies are mapped to 10 days, other currencies to 20 days and interest rate volatilities to 60 days; sovereign and SSA credit spreads rated investment grade are mapped to 20 days, covered bond and other corporate investment grade credit spreads to 40 days, high yield corporate credit spreads to 60 days and credit spread volatilities to 120 days; the most liquid FX pairs are mapped to 10 days, other pairs to 20 days and FX volatilities to 40 days. The appropriateness of the mapping is verified monthly through an automated check of all new risk factors and a review of changes in currency liquidity classification and issuer ratings, with the results recorded in the monthly liquidity horizon attestation (latest attestation 8 January 2027). The mapping table itself is documented in Annex A and in EVD-13-MDD section 4.2.1.

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: For a market data set, representativeness means that the risk factors capture the risks of the current portfolio and that the stress-period data represent the current portfolio's behaviour in stress. At 31 December 2026 the modelled risk factors capture 99.2% of the front-office interest rate delta (PV01), 98.1% of the credit spread sensitivity (CS01) and 97.4% of the vega of the IMA desks; the uncaptured remainder relates to basis and smile risk factors recorded in the RNIME inventory (EVD-13-MDD section 8.3). The reduced set explains on average 86% of the current full-set ES over the 60 business days to 31 December 2026, which confirms that the stress-period calibration is representative of the current risk profile. The PLA test results for Q4 2026 (four desks green, one amber) provide further evidence that the risk factor set is representative of the desks' front-office valuations. Detailed tables per desk and sensitivity type are presented in Annex B.

sections.heading: Data quality rules and thresholds
sections.text: For each critical data element at least one rule is defined for each applicable mandatory dimension, and the reason is recorded where a dimension does not apply (for example timeliness for static taxonomy fields). The 164 rules are documented in Annex A of EVD-13-DQ, and the 118 recurring rules are implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool, where they run daily on the production input data of the ES engine. Each rule has an amber and a red threshold; for market data the thresholds are stricter than the defaults of MRM-STD-022 §4.3: completeness after filling amber below 99.9% and red below 99.5%, accuracy against the secondary vendor amber above 0.2% and red above 0.5% of observations outside the instrument-specific tolerance, and timeliness amber if data for T are not available by 07:00 CET on T+1 and red if not available by 09:00 CET. sections.heading: Purpose and regulatory use
sections.text: The Market Risk – Expected Shortfall model (MDL-13, model version 3.0) calculates the own funds requirements for market risk of the Bank's trading desks under the alternative internal model approach of CRR Part Three, Title IV, Chapter 1b, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1623. It comprises the expected shortfall (ES) risk measure, the stress scenario risk measure (SSRM) for non-modellable risk factors, the default risk charge (DRC) and the back-testing and P&L attribution (PLA) framework that determines desk eligibility and the multiplication factor. Version 3.0 replaces the value-at-risk and stressed value-at-risk model (version 2.4) approved under Article 363 CRR, which remains in use for own funds requirements until the ECB grants permission under Article 325az CRR. Secondary uses are the daily VaR and ES limits of the trading desks, the monthly stress testing programme, the market risk component of the ICAAP and the daily risk report to the Management Board member responsible for risk, so that the model is the basis for reporting risk exposures to senior management. The model is developed and owned internally by Market Risk Modelling and is managed under MRM-POL-001; no component is acquired from a vendor, and the front-office pricing library used for revaluation is an internally developed and separately validated model.

The IMA scope comprises D01 EUR Rates Linear, D02 Rates Options, D03 G10 FX, D04 Credit Flow and D05 Covered Bonds and SSA, which together account for 83% of the trading book standardised own funds requirement. The rationale for including each desk rests on the availability of modellable risk factors, the expected PLA and back-testing performance over the 2025–2026 parallel run and the use of the ES in the desks' daily risk management; it is not motivated by a lower outcome than the alternative standardised approach, which is in fact lower than the IMA outcome for desks D01 and D05. D06 Equity Derivatives and D07 Emerging Markets Rates and FX remain under the alternative standardised approach because a high share of their risk factors fails the RFET. sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: The model consists of five components that run daily in the IMA engine: (1) the scenario generator, which builds ten-day overlapping historical shifts for the current and the stress window from the RFTS; (2) the revaluation layer, which revalues every position under every scenario with the front-office pricing library; (3) the ES aggregator, which applies liquidity horizon scaling, the reduced-set scaling ratio and the cross-category aggregation; (4) the SSRM module for non-modellable risk factors; and (5) the back-testing and PLA module. The DRC model runs weekly in a separate Monte Carlo engine that uses the same position and issuer data. ES is calculated for each IMA trading desk and for all IMA desks together. The own funds requirement is assembled in the capital module from the ES, SSRM, DRC, multiplication factor and PLA surcharge, as set out in section 4.2.3. No segmentation in the credit-model sense applies; the trading desk is the level at which performance is measured, eligibility is determined and results are reported.

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models and systems
sections.text: The model depends on the front-office pricing library FOPL version 7.4 (models registered as MDL-14 for derivatives valuation and on a separate inventory record for bond and linear pricers), on the IRB PD models for the DRC, and on the RFTS described in EVD-13-RDS. The ES engine calls the same pricing functions as the front office, so that risk-theoretical and hypothetical P&L differ only through the risk factors, not through the valuation models, which is the basis for the PLA test. Upstream systems are Apex (positions), the Market Data Repository (market data) and the Credit Rating System (IRB PDs); downstream systems are the capital calculation in the regulatory reporting system, the limit system and the risk reporting data mart. Model outputs are reconciled with the downstream regulatory reporting system at go-live and at least annually thereafter, as described in EVD-13-IMPL section 7. Changes to the pricing library are notified to Market Risk Modelling through the model change process so that their effect on ES and PLA can be assessed before release.

sections.heading: Calibration windows and samples
sections.text: The model uses three data windows: the current window of the most recent 12 months, which rolls forward daily; the stress window of 12 months, identified quarterly as described in section 5.1 and fixed between reviews; and the DRC correlation window of 20 years from 1 January 2007 to 31 December 2026. For the performance assessment, the equivalent of the out-of-time sample is the daily back-testing: each one-day VaR forecast is compared with P&L of the following day, which is not part of the calibration window used for that forecast, and the 2020–2026 period was used for a hypothetical back-test of the methodology before the parallel run. The windows were fixed in the development plan of 1 September 2025 before any calibration was performed. The stress window selection itself is not tested on the data on which it is performed; its robustness is assessed through the ranking of candidate windows and the sensitivity analysis in section 7.4.

sections.heading: Alternatives considered and selection rationale
sections.text: Four methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (compliance with Article 325bc CRR and PLA requirements, data availability, accuracy for non-linear products, stability of the capital figure, interpretability for the desks and implementation constraints): (a) historical simulation with full revaluation; (b) filtered historical simulation with EWMA volatility scaling; (c) Monte Carlo simulation with parametric risk factor distributions; and (d) a parametric delta-gamma-vega approach. Historical simulation with full revaluation was selected because it captures the joint empirical distribution of risk factors without distributional assumptions, gives the best PLA results for the option desks (Spearman correlation 0.78 for D02 against 0.61 for the delta-gamma-vega approach), reuses the validated VaR infrastructure and is readily explained to the desks. Filtered historical simulation produced a more responsive ES but a 24% higher day-to-day variability of the capital figure and is retained as challenger (section 7.3); Monte Carlo simulation required correlation and tail assumptions for 14,812 risk factors that could not be supported by the data; and the parametric approach failed the PLA test for D02 and D03. The selected method is also the most transparent of the four, so no additional controls under MRM-STD-020 §6.2 were required.

sections.heading: Expected shortfall calculation
sections.text: Partial expected shortfall measures are calculated daily for each desk and for all IMA desks together at the 97.5th percentile, one-tailed confidence level, as the average of the losses beyond that percentile of the P&L distribution obtained by full revaluation under the historical ten-day scenarios. With N scenarios in the window, the ES is the probability-weighted average of the largest losses with a total weight of 2.5% × N, the last loss being weighted fractionally; for N = 256 this is the six largest losses with full weight and the seventh with weight 0.4, divided by 6.4. Ten-day shifts are absolute for interest rates and credit spreads and relative (logarithmic) for FX rates and volatilities, applied to the current market state. The partial ES measures of the reduced set in the stress window are scaled by the ratio of the full-set to the reduced-set current ES, floored at 1, so that the stressed ES of a desk equals ES(reduced, stressed) × max(ES(full, current) / ES(reduced, current); 1). The positions in the Bank's own debt instruments on desk D05 (own covered bonds held for market making) are revalued with the Bank's own credit spread held constant, so that own credit spreads are excluded from the ES and from the SSRM.

sections.heading: Liquidity horizon scaling
sections.text: Partial ES is calculated with a base horizon of ten days and scaled to the liquidity horizons of 10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days: for each horizon j the ES is recomputed shocking only the risk factors whose liquidity horizon is equal to or longer than LH(j), and the liquidity-adjusted ES equals the square root of ES(10)² plus the sum over j ≥ 2 of (ES(j) × √((LH(j) − LH(j−1))/10))². The mapping of risk factors to broad categories, sub-categories and liquidity horizons follows Table 2 of Article 325bd CRR and is documented in the RFTS field LH_DAYS and in EVD-13-RDS section 4.5. At 31 December 2026 the liquidity adjustment increased the aggregated ES of the IMA desks by 38% compared with the ten-day ES, driven by the 40-day and 60-day horizons of the corporate credit spreads on D04 and D05 and by the 60-day horizon of the interest rate volatilities on D02. The monthly verification of the mapping is described in EVD-13-RDS section 4.5; a change in the liquidity classification of a currency or currency pair takes effect in the next daily run.

sections.heading: Stressed calibration and reduced set of risk factors
sections.text: The reduced set of 2,146 modellable risk factors was selected by ranking the full set by contribution to the current ES per desk and adding risk factors until the reduced set explains at least 75% of the current full-set ES; the ratio of reduced-set to full-set current ES is monitored daily, and over the 60 business days to 31 December 2026 it averaged 0.86 with a minimum of 0.81. A breach of the 75% threshold, measured as the average over the preceding 60 business days, is notified to the ECB immediately by Market Risk Management and remedied within two weeks by extending the reduced set, which is then documented as a change under MRM-STD-050. Stressed ES inputs are calibrated to the continuous 12-month stress period that maximises the reduced-set ES of the current portfolio, searched over the observation period starting on 1 January 2007, and the stress period is reviewed quarterly. Material changes to the reduced set of modellable risk factors require prior permission of the ECB under Article 325az(7) CRR, while other changes are notified; the change classification follows MRM-STD-050.

sections.heading: Aggregation across broad risk factor categories and own funds requirement
sections.text: The ES risk measure combines the unconstrained ES across all broad risk factor categories and the sum of the unconstrained ES per broad category with the supervisory correlation ρ = 50%: IMCC = ρ × UES(total) + (1 − ρ) × Σ UES(B). At 31 December 2026 the unconstrained ES was EUR 63.4 million for all categories together and EUR 58.9 million (interest rate), EUR 86.7 million (credit spread) and EUR 19.4 million (FX) per category, giving an IMCC of EUR 114.2 million. The own funds requirement for ES and SSRM equals the higher of the previous day's IMCC plus SSRM and the multiplication factor times the 60-business-day average IMCC plus the 60-business-day average SSRM: at 31 December 2026 max(114.2 + 26.1; 1.5 × 109.8 + 25.3) = EUR 190.0 million. The default risk charge is the higher of the most recent DRC and its average over the preceding 12 weeks (EUR 39.6 million against EUR 38.9 million), and the PLA surcharge for the amber desk D02 is EUR 6.1 million, so the total IMA own funds requirement is EUR 235.7 million, equivalent to EUR 2,946 million risk-weighted exposure amount.

sections.heading: Risk factor coverage and representation
sections.text: The risk-measurement model captures all risk factors of the standardised approach sensitivities for the IMA desks except 214 basis and smile risk factors, whose omission changes the PLA test statistics by less than 0.01 and is therefore immaterial; for every risk factor present in the pricing models but not in the risk model, the Bank maintains an explanation in the risk factor mapping register. Risk factors were selected from the inputs of the front-office pricing models, assessed for economic relevance to the desks' positions, availability of daily history and real price observations, and stability of their time series; the risk factor set is therefore driven by the pricing models rather than by statistical selection. The risk-measurement model captures correlation risk through the joint historical scenarios and basis risk through separate risk factors for each curve, index and issuer, including the €STR–EURIBOR tenor bases, cross-currency bases and bond–CDS bases. Risk factor coverage per desk and sensitivity type is shown in EVD-13-RDS Annex B.

sections.heading: Interest rate risk factors
sections.text: For interest rate exposures in EUR, USD and GBP, the material currencies of the IMA desks, the yield curves are modelled with twelve tenors (1 week, 1, 3 and 6 months, and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20 and 30 years), exceeding the minimum of six maturity segments. Spread risk between imperfectly correlated curves is captured through separate curves for €STR, EURIBOR 3M and 6M, SOFR, SONIA and the government bond curves of Germany, France, the Netherlands, Italy and Spain. Other currencies (CHF, JPY, SEK, NOK, DKK, CAD and AUD) are modelled with eight tenors. Interest rate volatilities are represented by SABR parameter surfaces for swaptions and caps and floors in EUR, USD and GBP on a grid of six expiries and six tenors; the reduced grid of the risk model compared with the front-office surface is the main structural HPL–RTPL difference for desk D02 (limitation L-13-02).

sections.heading: Credit spread risk factors and liquidity horizon mapping
sections.text: Credit spread risk factors comprise single-name CDS curves (5 tenors per name), bond-implied issuer spread curves for names without CDS, iTraxx and CDX index curves and the covered bond spread curves by issuer and rating. Covered bond credit spreads are mapped to the broad sub-category corporate investment grade with a liquidity horizon of 40 days, and SSA spreads rated investment grade to the sovereign investment grade sub-category with 20 days. The mapping of covered bonds is an expert judgement (EJ-13-01): Table 2 of Article 325bd CRR has no separate covered bond sub-category, and the corporate classification was chosen because covered bonds are issued by credit institutions; the alternative mapping to the sovereign sub-category (20 days) would reduce the IMCC by 3.2%. Credit spread volatilities are not material for the IMA desks and are mapped to 120 days where they occur. Rating changes that move an issuer between investment grade and high yield change the liquidity horizon in the next daily run.

sections.heading: Default risk charge
sections.text: The internal default risk model measures default losses of credit and equity positions of the IMA desks as a 99.9% value-at-risk over a one-year horizon with constant positions, and models the default of equity positions (none at present) as a price of zero. Defaults are simulated with a two-factor Gaussian copula (a global factor and a sector-region factor) over 5,000,000 scenarios, with default correlations calibrated to weekly equity returns and five-year CDS spread changes from 1 January 2007 to 31 December 2026, a 20-year period that includes the ES stress period, transformed to a one-year horizon. The two-factor structure was chosen over a single-factor model because it reproduces sector concentration in the credit flow and covered bond portfolios; the choice is justified in the calibration report and the correlation assumptions are transparent in the parameter file drc_corr_2026Q4. Default probabilities are floored at 0.03%, or at 0.01% for exposures eligible for a 0% risk weight and covered bonds eligible for a 10% risk weight. The DRC is calculated weekly on Friday positions and reported with the 12-week average.

sections.heading: Back-testing VaR and P&L attribution design
sections.text: The back-testing VaR uses a one-day holding period at the 99th and 97.5th percentiles, shocks only the modellable risk factors in the PLA risk factor list, is calibrated to the current 12-month window and otherwise uses the ES model assumptions. Overshootings are counted daily per desk and for all IMA desks together, separately for hypothetical and actual P&L. A desk meets the back-testing requirements if, over the latest 250 business days, it has no more than 12 overshootings at the 99th percentile and no more than 30 at the 97.5th percentile on both hypothetical and actual P&L; otherwise it leaves the IMA and is capitalised under the alternative standardised approach. The multiplication factor is 1.5 plus the add-on of Table 3 of Article 325bf(6) CRR (0.00 below 5, 0.20 for 5, 0.26 for 6, 0.33 for 7, 0.38 for 8, 0.42 for 9 and 0.50 for more than 9 overshootings), based on the higher of the hypothetical and actual 99% VaR overshootings of all IMA desks over 250 business days. The PLA test compares RTPL and HPL per desk quarterly on 250 business days with the Spearman correlation and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/2059: green if Spearman is at least 0.80 and KS at most 0.09, red if Spearman is below 0.70 or KS above 0.12, amber otherwise; red desks are capitalised under the standardised approach and amber desks attract the capital surcharge for all positions on the desk. The precise list of risk factors used for back-testing and PLA is version-controlled in the PLA risk factor list (current version PLA-RFL-2026Q4, 14,431 risk factors), derived from the PLA results, and every change is tracked with date, reason and approver.

sections.heading: Calibration of the stress period
sections.text: The stress period is identified by computing, for every 12-month window between 1 January 2007 and the review date, the reduced-set ES of the current portfolio and selecting the window with the maximum. At the Q4 2026 review of 12 January 2027 the selected window was 8 September 2008 to 4 September 2009 with a stressed reduced-set ES of EUR 55.1 million; the second-ranked window, 4 March 2022 to 3 March 2023, reached 91% of this value. The review is performed quarterly and additionally when the portfolio changes materially; the stress period has not changed since the Q1 2025 review. sections.heading: DRC calibration
sections.text: DRC default probabilities are taken from the IRB rating system of record where an IRB PD exists (1,146 of 1,882 issuers) and otherwise from long-run rating agency default rates over 1981–2025, i.e. more than five years of historical default data; they are not inferred solely from current market prices, and the source of each PD is documented in the field PD_SOURCE. LGDs are taken from the IRB LGD models where available and otherwise set at 60% for senior unsecured bonds, 80% for subordinated bonds and 25% for covered bonds (EJ-13-07). Factor loadings are estimated per issuer by regressing weekly equity returns, or CDS spread changes where no listed equity exists, on the global and sector-region factors, and are capped at 0.85. The correlation calibration is refreshed annually; the 2026 calibration increased the average pairwise asset correlation from 0.21 to 0.23 and the DRC by 4.1%. Sovereign issuers are included in the simulation with their own PDs and loadings.

sections.heading: Benchmarking and challenger model
sections.text: The ES model is compared with a challenger based on filtered historical simulation (EWMA volatility scaling with λ = 0.97) and with the previous model version (VaR and stressed VaR). Over 2026 the challenger's current ES was on average 7% higher than the historical simulation ES because of volatility clustering in the second quarter, whereas its stressed ES was 3% lower; the challenger does not outperform the model in back-testing (5 against 4 overshootings at 99% on actual P&L) and the difference is explained by the volatility scaling. Against the previous model, the IMA own funds requirement of EUR 235.7 million is 10.1% higher than the Article 363 requirement of EUR 214.0 million at 31 December 2026, mainly because of the liquidity horizons for credit spreads. The model is also benchmarked annually through the supervisory benchmarking portfolios of the EBA, for which the Bank submits the results of its internal approach for the hypothetical portfolios together with an explanation of the methodologies used; in the 2026 exercise the Bank's ES was within the interquartile range for 22 of 26 portfolios, and the analysis of the four outliers attributes them to the covered bond liquidity horizon and the SABR grid.

sections.heading: Stress testing programme
sections.text: A stress testing programme covering the internal model runs daily with 18 historical and 12 hypothetical scenarios on the IMA desks, complemented by a monthly reverse stress test that identifies the scenarios that would exhaust the trading book loss limit of EUR 250 million; the results are reviewed by the Market Risk Committee, on which senior management is represented, at least monthly. The hypothetical scenarios include a 200 basis point parallel shift of the EUR curve, a widening of covered bond spreads by 150 basis points and a 20% depreciation of the euro against the US dollar. Stress results are also used to challenge the stress period selection: no historical scenario produced a larger ten-day loss than the ES stress window.

sections.heading: Climate and environmental risk
sections.text: The materiality of climate-related and environmental risks for the model was assessed in the 2026 model review: transition and physical risks affect the model through market prices (credit spreads of carbon-intensive issuers and covered bond spreads in flood-exposed regions), which are captured in the historical scenarios, and the Bank's climate stress scenarios are run on the IMA desks as part of the stress testing programme. The assessment concluded that no separate climate risk driver is required in the ES or DRC because the IMA portfolio has limited exposure to carbon-intensive sectors (2.8% of credit spread sensitivity) and because the relevant effects are reflected in market data; the assessment is repeated annually.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: The material assumptions of the model are identified and assessed for plausibility: (i) the historical ten-day shifts of the current and stress windows represent plausible future moves; (ii) the stress period identified with the reduced set is also the stress period of the full set; (iii) proxies represent the stress behaviour of risk factors without history; (iv) the liquidity horizons of Table 2 reflect the time to exit positions in stressed markets; (v) positions are constant over the horizon; and (vi) the DRC factor model captures default dependence. Assumption (ii) is supported by the reduced-set ratio of 0.86; assumption (iii) by the proxy track record tests; assumption (iv) is regulatory; assumption (v) is conservative for a portfolio that is actively hedged. The documentation of methodology, assumptions and limitations in this document, together with the RFTS documentation, is intended to enable a qualified third party to understand the model and to replicate its calibration and implementation.

sections.heading: Escalation of monitoring results
sections.text: Each amber result is analysed by the model owner and its cause documented in the quarterly monitoring report. The action plan proposes no action with justification, a temporary overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use, with any change processed under MRM-STD-050. Numerous overshootings indicating that the model is not sufficiently accurate lead to a model review by Market Risk Modelling and, where confirmed, to a model improvement proposal under MRM-STD-050. Firm-wide overshootings that determine the multiplier add-on are reported to the Market Risk Committee monthly, and overshootings are explained within five business days and notified to the ECB within the same deadline.

sections.heading: Purpose and regulatory use
sections.text: The Market Risk – Expected Shortfall model (MDL-13, model version 3.0) calculates the own funds requirements for market risk of the Bank's trading desks under the alternative internal model approach of CRR Part Three, Title IV, Chapter 1b, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1623. It comprises the expected shortfall (ES) risk measure, the stress scenario risk measure (SSRM) for non-modellable risk factors, the default risk charge (DRC) and the back-testing and P&L attribution (PLA) framework that determines desk eligibility and the multiplication factor. Version 3.0 replaces the value-at-risk and stressed value-at-risk model (version 2.4) approved under Article 363 CRR, which remains in use for own funds requirements until the ECB grants permission under Article 325az CRR. Secondary uses are the daily VaR and ES limits of the trading desks, the monthly stress testing programme, the market risk component of the ICAAP and the daily risk report to the Management Board member responsible for risk, so that the model is the basis for reporting risk exposures to senior management. The model is developed and owned internally by Market Risk Modelling and is managed under MRM-POL-001; no component is acquired from a vendor, and the front-office pricing library used for revaluation is an internally developed and separately validated model.

sections.heading: Scope of application and trading desk structure
sections.text: The trading book is organised in seven trading desks, each with a documented business strategy, risk limits and a head of desk, approved by the Market Risk Committee on 11 June 2026; every position is assigned to one desk only, in line with the desk's business strategy, and is managed and monitored on that desk. The IMA scope comprises D01 EUR Rates Linear, D02 Rates Options, D03 G10 FX, D04 Credit Flow and D05 Covered Bonds and SSA, which together account for 83% of the trading book standardised own funds requirement. The rationale for including each desk rests on the availability of modellable risk factors, the expected PLA and back-testing performance over the 2025–2026 parallel run and the use of the ES in the desks' daily risk management; it is not motivated by a lower outcome than the alternative standardised approach, which is in fact lower than the IMA outcome for desks D01 and D05. D06 Equity Derivatives and D07 Emerging Markets Rates and FX remain under the alternative standardised approach because a high share of their risk factors fails the RFET. The model assigned to each desk, the desk limits and the business strategies are recorded in the desk mandate register referenced in the Market Risk Committee decision MaRC-2026-06-04.

sections.heading: Model structure and components
sections.text: The model consists of five components that run daily in the IMA engine: (1) the scenario generator, which builds ten-day overlapping historical shifts for the current and the stress window from the RFTS; (2) the revaluation layer, which revalues every position under every scenario with the front-office pricing library; (3) the ES aggregator, which applies liquidity horizon scaling, the reduced-set scaling ratio and the cross-category aggregation; (4) the SSRM module for non-modellable risk factors; and (5) the back-testing and PLA module. The DRC model runs weekly in a separate Monte Carlo engine that uses the same position and issuer data. ES is calculated for each IMA trading desk and for all IMA desks together. The own funds requirement is assembled in the capital module from the ES, SSRM, DRC, multiplication factor and PLA surcharge, as set out in section 4.2.3. No segmentation in the credit-model sense applies; the trading desk is the level at which performance is measured, eligibility is determined and results are reported.

sections.heading: Dependencies on other models and systems
sections.text: The model depends on the front-office pricing library FOPL version 7.4 (models registered as MDL-14 for derivatives valuation and on a separate inventory record for bond and linear pricers), on the IRB PD models for the DRC, and on the RFTS described in EVD-13-RDS. The ES engine calls the same pricing functions as the front office, so that risk-theoretical and hypothetical P&L differ only through the risk factors, not through the valuation models, which is the basis for the PLA test. Upstream systems are Apex (positions), the Market Data Repository (market data) and the Credit Rating System (IRB PDs); downstream systems are the capital calculation in the regulatory reporting system, the limit system and the risk reporting data mart. Model outputs are reconciled with the downstream regulatory reporting system at go-live and at least annually thereafter, as described in EVD-13-IMPL section 7. Changes to the pricing library are notified to Market Risk Modelling through the model change process so that their effect on ES and PLA can be assessed before release.

sections.heading: Calibration windows and samples
sections.text: The model uses three data windows: the current window of the most recent 12 months, which rolls forward daily; the stress window of 12 months, identified quarterly as described in section 5.1 and fixed between reviews; and the DRC correlation window of 20 years from 1 January 2007 to 31 December 2026. For the performance assessment, the equivalent of the out-of-time sample is the daily back-testing: each one-day VaR forecast is compared with P&L of the following day, which is not part of the calibration window used for that forecast, and the 2020–2026 period was used for a hypothetical back-test of the methodology before the parallel run. The windows were fixed in the development plan of 1 September 2025 before any calibration was performed. The stress window selection itself is not tested on the data on which it is performed; its robustness is assessed through the ranking of candidate windows and the sensitivity analysis in section 7.4.

sections.heading: Alternatives considered and selection rationale
sections.text: Four methodologies were assessed against documented criteria (compliance with Article 325bc CRR and PLA requirements, data availability, accuracy for non-linear products, stability of the capital figure, interpretability for the desks and implementation constraints): (a) historical simulation with full revaluation; (b) filtered historical simulation with EWMA volatility scaling; (c) Monte Carlo simulation with parametric risk factor distributions; and (d) a parametric delta-gamma-vega approach. Historical simulation with full revaluation was selected because it captures the joint empirical distribution of risk factors without distributional assumptions, gives the best PLA results for the option desks (Spearman correlation 0.78 for D02 against 0.61 for the delta-gamma-vega approach), reuses the validated VaR infrastructure and is readily explained to the desks. Filtered historical simulation produced a more responsive ES but a 24% higher day-to-day variability of the capital figure and is retained as challenger (section 7.3); Monte Carlo simulation required correlation and tail assumptions for 14,812 risk factors that could not be supported by the data; and the parametric approach failed the PLA test for D02 and D03. The selected method is also the most transparent of the four, so no additional controls under MRM-STD-020 §6.2 were required.

sections.heading: Expected shortfall calculation
sections.text: Partial expected shortfall measures are calculated daily for each desk and for all IMA desks together at the 97.5th percentile, one-tailed confidence level, as the average of the losses beyond that percentile of the P&L distribution obtained by full revaluation under the historical ten-day scenarios. With N scenarios in the window, the ES is the probability-weighted average of the largest losses with a total weight of 2.5% × N, the last loss being weighted fractionally; for N = 256 this is the six largest losses with full weight and the seventh with weight 0.4, divided by 6.4. Ten-day shifts are absolute for interest rates and credit spreads and relative (logarithmic) for FX rates and volatilities, applied to the current market state. The partial ES measures of the reduced set in the stress window are scaled by the ratio of the full-set to the reduced-set current ES, floored at 1, so that the stressed ES of a desk equals ES(reduced, stressed) × max(ES(full, current) / ES(reduced, current); 1). The positions in the Bank's own debt instruments on desk D05 (own covered bonds held for market making) are revalued with the Bank's own credit spread held constant, so that own credit spreads are excluded from the ES and from the SSRM.

sections.heading: Liquidity horizon scaling
sections.text: Partial ES is calculated with a base horizon of ten days and scaled to the liquidity horizons of 10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days: for each horizon j the ES is recomputed shocking only the risk factors whose liquidity horizon is equal to or longer than LH(j), and the liquidity-adjusted ES equals the square root of ES(10)² plus the sum over j ≥ 2 of (ES(j) × √((LH(j) − LH(j−1))/10))². The mapping of risk factors to broad categories, sub-categories and liquidity horizons follows Table 2 of Article 325bd CRR and is documented in the RFTS field LH_DAYS and in EVD-13-RDS section 4.5. At 31 December 2026 the liquidity adjustment increased the aggregated ES of the IMA desks by 38% compared with the ten-day ES, driven by the 40-day and 60-day horizons of the corporate credit spreads on D04 and D05 and by the 60-day horizon of the interest rate volatilities on D02. The monthly verification of the mapping is described in EVD-13-RDS section 4.5; a change in the liquidity classification of a currency or currency pair takes effect in the next daily run.

sections.heading: Stressed calibration and reduced set of risk factors
sections.text: The reduced set of 2,146 modellable risk factors was selected by ranking the full set by contribution to the current ES per desk and adding risk factors until the reduced set explains at least 75% of the current full-set ES; the ratio of reduced-set to full-set current ES is monitored daily, and over the 60 business days to 31 December 2026 it averaged 0.86 with a minimum of 0.81. A breach of the 75% threshold, measured as the average over the preceding 60 business days, is notified to the ECB immediately by Market Risk Management and remedied within two weeks by extending the reduced set, which is then documented as a change under MRM-STD-050. Stressed ES inputs are calibrated to the continuous 12-month stress period that maximises the reduced-set ES of the current portfolio, searched over the observation period starting on 1 January 2007, and the stress period is reviewed quarterly. Material changes to the reduced set of modellable risk factors require prior permission of the ECB under Article 325az(7) CRR, while other changes are notified; the change classification follows MRM-STD-050.

sections.heading: Aggregation across broad risk factor categories and own funds requirement
sections.text: The ES risk measure combines the unconstrained ES across all broad risk factor categories and the sum of the unconstrained ES per broad category with the supervisory correlation ρ = 50%: IMCC = ρ × UES(total) + (1 − ρ) × Σ UES(B). At 31 December 2026 the unconstrained ES was EUR 63.4 million for all categories together and EUR 58.9 million (interest rate), EUR 86.7 million (credit spread) and EUR 19.4 million (FX) per category, giving an IMCC of EUR 114.2 million. The own funds requirement for ES and SSRM equals the higher of the previous day's IMCC plus SSRM and the multiplication factor times the 60-business-day average IMCC plus the 60-business-day average SSRM: at 31 December 2026 max(114.2 + 26.1; 1.5 × 109.8 + 25.3) = EUR 190.0 million. The default risk charge is the higher of the most recent DRC and its average over the preceding 12 weeks (EUR 39.6 million against EUR 38.9 million), and the PLA surcharge for the amber desk D02 is EUR 6.1 million, so the total IMA own funds requirement is EUR 235.7 million, equivalent to EUR 2,946 million risk-weighted exposure amount.

sections.heading: Risk factor coverage and representation
sections.text: The risk-measurement model captures all risk factors of the standardised approach sensitivities for the IMA desks except 214 basis and smile risk factors, whose omission changes the PLA test statistics by less than 0.01 and is therefore immaterial; for every risk factor present in the pricing models but not in the risk model, the Bank maintains an explanation in the risk factor mapping register. Risk factors were selected from the inputs of the front-office pricing models, assessed for economic relevance to the desks' positions, availability of daily history and real price observations, and stability of their time series; the risk factor set is therefore driven by the pricing models rather than by statistical selection. The risk-measurement model captures correlation risk through the joint historical scenarios and basis risk through separate risk factors for each curve, index and issuer, including the €STR–EURIBOR tenor bases, cross-currency bases and bond–CDS bases. Risk factor coverage per desk and sensitivity type is shown in EVD-13-RDS Annex B.

sections.heading: Interest rate risk factors
sections.text: For interest rate exposures in EUR, USD and GBP, the material currencies of the IMA desks, the yield curves are modelled with twelve tenors (1 week, 1, 3 and 6 months, and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20 and 30 years), exceeding the minimum of six maturity segments. Spread risk between imperfectly correlated curves is captured through separate curves for €STR, EURIBOR 3M and 6M, SOFR, SONIA and the government bond curves of Germany, France, the Netherlands, Italy and Spain. Other currencies (CHF, JPY, SEK, NOK, DKK, CAD and AUD) are modelled with eight tenors. Interest rate volatilities are represented by SABR parameter surfaces for swaptions and caps and floors in EUR, USD and GBP on a grid of six expiries and six tenors; the reduced grid of the risk model compared with the front-office surface is the main structural HPL–RTPL difference for desk D02 (limitation L-13-02).

sections.heading: Credit spread risk factors and liquidity horizon mapping
sections.text: Credit spread risk factors comprise single-name CDS curves (5 tenors per name), bond-implied issuer spread curves for names without CDS, iTraxx and CDX index curves and the covered bond spread curves by issuer and rating. Covered bond credit spreads are mapped to the broad sub-category corporate investment grade with a liquidity horizon of 40 days, and SSA spreads rated investment grade to the sovereign investment grade sub-category with 20 days. The mapping of covered bonds is an expert judgement (EJ-13-01): Table 2 of Article 325bd CRR has no separate covered bond sub-category, and the corporate classification was chosen because covered bonds are issued by credit institutions; the alternative mapping to the sovereign sub-category (20 days) would reduce the IMCC by 3.2%. Credit spread volatilities are not material for the IMA desks and are mapped to 120 days where they occur. Rating changes that move an issuer between investment grade and high yield change the liquidity horizon in the next daily run.

sections.heading: Non-linear products and revaluation
sections.text: Swaptions, caps, floors and callable bonds on desks D02 and D05 are fully revalued under every scenario with the front-office pricing library, which captures the non-linearity of options. FX options on desk D03 are revalued with a spot-volatility grid of 11 spot and 9 volatility points per currency pair with interpolation between grid points; the approximation is justified by quantitative evidence: against full revaluation on 250 business days of 2026 the grid produced a maximum ES error of 0.6% and a mean absolute error of 0.2% of the desk ES. Linear products (swaps, bonds, FX forwards and CDS) are fully revalued as well, since the revaluation cost is low. The grid resolution is an expert judgement (EJ-13-03) and is reviewed annually against full revaluation.

sections.heading: Non-modellable risk factors and stress scenario risk measure
sections.text: Risk factors are assessed for modellability quarterly with the RFET of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/2060 on the real price observations of the preceding twelve months, requiring at least 24 observations with no 90-day period of fewer than four observations, or at least 100 observations; the Bank uses its own bucketing aligned with the risk factor tenors. Own funds requirements for the 381 risk factors assessed as non-modellable at the Q4 2026 assessment are calculated with the stress scenario risk measure of Article 325bk CRR. For each non-modellable risk factor an extreme scenario of future shock is calibrated to the stress period at a level at least as prudent as the ES, using the ES-equivalent loss of the stressed ten-day shifts scaled to the liquidity horizon of the risk factor; where the risk factor has no history in the stress period, the shock is derived from the available history and scaled by the ratio of stressed to current volatility of its proxy, floored at 1 (EJ-13-06). The 212 idiosyncratic credit spread NMRFs are aggregated with zero correlation, and the remaining 169 NMRFs with a correlation of 0.6 in the aggregation formula of the RTS on the stress scenario risk measure; these correlation assumptions are documented and reviewed annually. At 31 December 2026 the SSRM amounted to EUR 26.1 million, of which 58% relates to single-name credit spreads on D04.

sections.heading: Default risk charge
sections.text: The internal default risk model measures default losses of credit and equity positions of the IMA desks as a 99.9% value-at-risk over a one-year horizon with constant positions, and models the default of equity positions (none at present) as a price of zero. Defaults are simulated with a two-factor Gaussian copula (a global factor and a sector-region factor) over 5,000,000 scenarios, with default correlations calibrated to weekly equity returns and five-year CDS spread changes from 1 January 2007 to 31 December 2026, a 20-year period that includes the ES stress period, transformed to a one-year horizon. The two-factor structure was chosen over a single-factor model because it reproduces sector concentration in the credit flow and covered bond portfolios; the choice is justified in the calibration report and the correlation assumptions are transparent in the parameter file drc_corr_2026Q4. Default probabilities are floored at 0.03%, or at 0.01% for exposures eligible for a 0% risk weight and covered bonds eligible for a 10% risk weight. The DRC is calculated weekly on Friday positions and reported with the 12-week average.

sections.heading: Back-testing VaR and P&L attribution design
sections.text: The back-testing VaR uses a one-day holding period at the 99th and 97.5th percentiles, shocks only the modellable risk factors in the PLA risk factor list, is calibrated to the current 12-month window and otherwise uses the ES model assumptions. Overshootings are counted daily per desk and for all IMA desks together, separately for hypothetical and actual P&L. A desk meets the back-testing requirements if, over the latest 250 business days, it has no more than 12 overshootings at the 99th percentile and no more than 30 at the 97.5th percentile on both hypothetical and actual P&L; otherwise it leaves the IMA and is capitalised under the alternative standardised approach. The multiplication factor is 1.5 plus the add-on of Table 3 of Article 325bf(6) CRR (0.00 below 5, 0.20 for 5, 0.26 for 6, 0.33 for 7, 0.38 for 8, 0.42 for 9 and 0.50 for more than 9 overshootings), based on the higher of the hypothetical and actual 99% VaR overshootings of all IMA desks over 250 business days. The PLA test compares RTPL and HPL per desk quarterly on 250 business days with the Spearman correlation and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic under Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/2059: green if Spearman is at least 0.80 and KS at most 0.09, red if Spearman is below 0.70 or KS above 0.12, amber otherwise; red desks are capitalised under the standardised approach and amber desks attract the capital surcharge for all positions on the desk. The precise list of risk factors used for back-testing and PLA is version-controlled in the PLA risk factor list (current version PLA-RFL-2026Q4, 14,431 risk factors), derived from the PLA results, and every change is tracked with date, reason and approver.

sections.heading: Calibration of the stress period
sections.text: The stress period is identified by computing, for every 12-month window between 1 January 2007 and the review date, the reduced-set ES of the current portfolio and selecting the window with the maximum. At the Q4 2026 review of 12 January 2027 the selected window was 8 September 2008 to 4 September 2009 with a stressed reduced-set ES of EUR 55.1 million; the second-ranked window, 4 March 2022 to 3 March 2023, reached 91% of this value. The review is performed quarterly and additionally when the portfolio changes materially; the stress period has not changed since the Q1 2025 review. A change of stress period is approved by the model owner and reported to the Market Risk Committee and to Model Validation, and the stressed ES is recalculated from the next business day. Stress period reviews are produced with the tagged code version and archived with their input data, so that each review can be reproduced.

sections.text: DRC default probabilities are taken from the IRB rating system of record where an IRB PD exists (1,146 of 1,882 issuers) and otherwise from long-run rating agency default rates over 1981–2025, i.e. more than five years of historical default data; they are not inferred solely from current market prices, and the source of each PD is documented in the field PD_SOURCE. LGDs are taken from the IRB LGD models where available and otherwise set at 60% for senior unsecured bonds, 80% for subordinated bonds and 25% for covered bonds (EJ-13-07). Factor loadings are estimated per issuer by regressing weekly equity returns, or CDS spread changes where no listed equity exists, on the global and sector-region factors, and are capped at 0.85. The correlation calibration is refreshed annually; the 2026 calibration increased the average pairwise asset correlation from 0.21 to 0.23 and the DRC by 4.1%. Sovereign issuers are included in the simulation with their own PDs and loadings.

sections.heading: Margin of conservatism
sections.text: Not applicable.
