sections.heading: Back-testing performance
sections.text: Over the 250 business days to 31 December 2026 the IMA desks together recorded 3 overshootings at the 99th percentile on hypothetical P&L and 4 on actual P&L, so the add-on is 0.00 and the multiplication factor 1.5. Per desk, the 99% overshootings on hypothetical/actual P&L were D01 2/2, D02 4/5, D03 1/2, D04 5/6 and D05 1/1, and the 97.5% overshootings D01 5/6, D02 9/11, D03 4/5, D04 12/14 and D05 3/4, all well within the thresholds of 12 and 30. Kupiec proportion-of-failures and Christoffersen independence tests at the 99% level do not reject the model at the 5% significance level for any desk or for the top of the house. The detailed quarterly results, including the explanation of each overshooting, are reported in the back-testing and PLA report EVD-13-BT.

sections.heading: Benchmarking and challenger model
sections.text: The ES model is compared with a challenger based on filtered historical simulation (EWMA volatility scaling with λ = 0.97) and with the previous model version (VaR and stressed VaR). Over 2026 the challenger's current ES was on average 7% higher than the historical simulation ES because of volatility clustering in the second quarter, whereas its stressed ES was 3% lower; the challenger does not outperform the model in back-testing (5 against 4 overshootings at 99% on actual P&L) and the difference is explained by the volatility scaling. Against the previous model, the IMA own funds requirement of EUR 235.7 million is 10.1% higher than the Article 363 requirement of EUR 214.0 million at 31 December 2026, mainly because of the liquidity horizons for credit spreads. The model is also benchmarked annually through the supervisory benchmarking portfolios of the EBA, for which the Bank submits the results of its internal approach for the hypothetical portfolios together with an explanation of the methodologies used; in the 2026 exercise the Bank's ES was within the interquartile range for 22 of 26 portfolios, and the analysis of the four outliers attributes them to the covered bond liquidity horizon and the SABR grid.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses covered the key assumptions, parameters and inputs of the model at 31 December 2026: using the second-ranked stress window (March 2022 to March 2023) reduces the stressed ES by 9.0%; raising the proxy beta floor from 1.0 to 1.2 increases it by 1.9%; filling gaps by carrying forward the last value instead of interpolation reduces it by 0.3%; replacing the FX option grid by full revaluation increases the D03 ES by 0.4%; and reducing the reduced set by 10% of its risk factors lowers the reduced-set ratio from 0.86 to 0.83. The material expert judgements were tested under reasonable alternatives: mapping covered bonds to the sovereign sub-category (EJ-13-01) reduces the IMCC by 3.2%, and using the iBoxx index without beta scaling for the CDS proxies (EJ-13-04) reduces the stressed reduced-set ES by 1.6%. None of the sensitivities changes the eligibility of a desk or the multiplication factor.

sections.heading: Stress testing programme
sections.text: A stress testing programme covering the internal model runs daily with 18 historical and 12 hypothetical scenarios on the IMA desks, complemented by a monthly reverse stress test that identifies the scenarios that would exhaust the trading book loss limit of EUR 250 million; the results are reviewed by the Market Risk Committee, on which senior management is represented, at least monthly. The hypothetical scenarios include a 200 basis point parallel shift of the EUR curve, a widening of covered bond spreads by 150 basis points and a 20% depreciation of the euro against the US dollar. Stress results are also used to challenge the stress period selection: no historical scenario produced a larger ten-day loss than the ES stress window.

sections.heading: Climate and environmental risk
sections.text: The materiality of climate-related and environmental risks for the model was assessed in the 2026 model review: transition and physical risks affect the model through market prices (credit spreads of carbon-intensive issuers and covered bond spreads in flood-exposed regions), which are captured in the historical scenarios, and the Bank's climate stress scenarios are run on the IMA desks as part of the stress testing programme. The assessment concluded that no separate climate risk driver is required in the ES or DRC because the IMA portfolio has limited exposure to carbon-intensive sectors (2.8% of credit spread sensitivity) and because the relevant effects are reflected in market data; the assessment is repeated annually.

sections.heading: Material assumptions
sections.text: The material assumptions of the model are identified and assessed for plausibility: (i) the historical ten-day shifts of the current and stress windows represent plausible future moves; (ii) the stress period identified with the reduced set is also the stress period of the full set; (iii) proxies represent the stress behaviour of risk factors without history; (iv) the liquidity horizons of Table 2 reflect the time to exit positions in stressed markets; (v) positions are constant over the horizon; and (vi) the DRC factor model captures default dependence. Assumption (ii) is supported by the reduced-set ratio of 0.86; assumption (iii) by the proxy track record tests; assumption (iv) is regulatory; assumption (v) is conservative for a portfolio that is actively hedged. The documentation of methodology, assumptions and limitations in this document, together with the RFTS documentation, is intended to enable a qualified third party to understand the model and to replicate its calibration and implementation.

sections.heading: Risks not in the model engines
sections.text: The RNIME framework, owned by Market Risk Management, defines the policies and controls for identifying, quantifying and managing risks not captured in the model engines, with the tasks of Market Risk Modelling (identification and quantification), Market Risk Management (approval and reporting) and Model Validation (review), and quarterly quantification and reporting. At 31 December 2026 the RNIME inventory contained 23 items with a total estimated impact of EUR 7.9 million on the IMCC, the largest being the SABR smile beyond the risk model grid (EUR 2.6 million), cross-currency basis beyond 30 years (EUR 1.1 million) and dividend risk on convertible hedges (EUR 0.9 million). RNIME items above EUR 1 million are included in the Pillar 2 market risk assessment of the ICAAP and linked to the remediation of limitation L-13-02. The RNIME inventory is also the reference for the risk factors present in pricing but not in the risk model (section 4.3).

sections.heading: Expert judgement log
sections.text: The expert judgement log is stored with the model documentation in MRM DocHub and records every expert judgement with its type, life cycle stage and affected parameter. The entries are: EJ-13-01 liquidity horizon mapping of covered bonds (design; +3.2% IMCC against the sovereign alternative; high materiality); EJ-13-02 five-day limit for interpolation of gaps (data treatment; −0.3%; low); EJ-13-03 FX option grid resolution (design; +0.4% D03 ES; low); EJ-13-04 CDS proxy hierarchy (data treatment; +1.6% stressed ES; medium); EJ-13-05 proxy beta floor of 1.0 (data treatment; +0.9%; low); EJ-13-06 SSRM scaling of short histories (calibration; not quantifiable, therefore high); EJ-13-07 DRC LGDs for issuers without IRB LGD (calibration; +2.2% DRC; low). Each entry records the rationale, the evidence relied on and the alternatives considered and rejected; for example, EJ-13-01 documents that the sovereign mapping was rejected because covered bonds of the same issuer showed 2.4 times the bid-ask widening of sovereign bonds in March 2020. sections.heading: Validation, approval and supervisory permission
sections.text: Model Validation – Market & ALM, a unit separate from Market Risk Management and Market Risk Modelling, performs the initial validation of version 3.0 (VAL-2027-MR-03) and the annual validation of the IMA models, with staff who did not contribute to the development and whose remuneration is not linked to model approval. Market Risk Management, the independent risk control unit reporting to the Chief Risk Officer, owns the overall risk management system, produces the daily reports on model output and limits and approved the design of the IMA models, which are developed in Market Risk Modelling under its oversight. The internal models are validated at initial development, after significant changes, at least annually and after significant structural changes in the market or the portfolio, and the validation goes beyond regulatory back-testing and PLA to test model assumptions, own back-testing relevant to portfolio risks and hypothetical portfolios covering basis, concentration and proxy risks. The validation of the DRC verifies correlation and systematic factor choices and applies stress and sensitivity tests beyond past events with quantitative benchmarks. The validation opinion, this document, the self-assessment, open findings and limitations will be submitted to the Model Risk Committee for approval at gate G3, planned for 1 July 2027; the internal approval precedes the application to the ECB, and version 3.0 will be used for own funds requirements only after the ECB has granted permission.

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This report documents the data quality assessment of the frozen market data and risk factor time series data set RFTS-2026Q4-F1 used for the development and calibration of the ES model version 3.0 (MDL-13), performed under MRM-STD-022 before the data set was frozen. The assessment covers all critical data elements: the 2,146 reduced-set time series over 1 December 2006 to 31 December 2026, the 12,666 further risk factors over the 2026 window, the RFET observation counts, the IRB and external PDs used by the DRC, and the HPL and APL of the five IMA desks for 2026. The data are governed under DATA-POL-001, which applies the principles of the ECB Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting to all data used as model inputs, with data ownership, lineage, quality rules and issue management in place for every source domain. The assessment was performed jointly by Market Risk Modelling and the Data Stewards of Market Data Services and Product Control between 11 January and 3 February 2027.

sections.heading: Completeness
sections.text: Completeness is measured at record level, as the share of expected risk factor-days, positions and desk-days present in the RFTS, and at attribute level, as the share of non-missing values per variable. At record level, 100% of the positions of the IMA desks in Apex at 31 December 2026 and 100% of the 1,250 desk-days of HPL and APL are present; all 14,812 risk factors to which the IMA positions are sensitive are included. At attribute level, raw completeness of the reduced-set time series is 99.83% in the 2026 window and 97.4% in the 2008–2009 stress window; after the documented interpolation and proxies, completeness is 100% in both windows. Two rules are amber: the completeness of the NOK and SEK swaption volatility surfaces (99.7% after filling, against the amber threshold of 99.9%); all other rules are green. Completeness gaps are identified and their impact on the reliability of the ES is assessed in the deficiency log (section 9).

sections.heading: Accuracy
sections.text: Accuracy is measured by reconciliation of positions and P&L to the source systems and the general ledger, by comparison of risk factor values with an independent secondary vendor, and by sample-based checks against source documentation. As MDL-13 is a Tier 1 model, the assessment included a sample-based verification of 250 randomly selected risk factor observations against the original vendor files and broker quote records, and of 60 real price observations against trade confirmations; no error was found. Positions reconcile with the general ledger within 0.002% of gross absolute market value and HPL and APL with the official desk P&L within EUR 1,000 per desk-day, except for the two desk-days of DD-13-04, which were corrected at source. Against the secondary vendor, 0.07% of reduced-set observations in 2026 were outside the instrument-specific tolerance (0.5 basis point for rates, 2 basis points for credit spreads, 0.05% for FX spot), below the amber threshold of 0.2%.

sections.heading: Consistency
sections.text: Consistency was assessed between the RFTS and the production input data of the ES engine, over the observation period and as logical consistency between related fields. The development and production inputs are generated by the same build code; a comparison of the 31 December 2026 production input with the frozen RFTS showed no difference. Over the observation period, the benchmark transitions (EONIA to €STR, LIBOR to risk-free rates) and the 2014 migration from RiskStore to the MDR were checked for breaks in level and volatility; the €STR reconstruction by EONIA minus 8.5 basis points produces no break at 1 October 2019. Logical rules check monotonic discount factors, positive hazard rates, consistency of CDS term structures and the absence of calendar arbitrage in volatility surfaces; 99.4% of records pass, above the amber threshold of 99%, and the swaption smile rule is assessed against the approved thresholds of DQ-DEV-2027-02.

sections.heading: Timeliness
sections.text: Timeliness is measured as the lag between the end-of-day close and availability in the MDR and as the currency of periodically refreshed items (quarterly RFET counts and IRB PDs, which are refreshed monthly). In 2026, data were available by 07:00 CET on 253 of 256 business days and by 09:00 CET on all days, so the ES was reported by the 10:00 CET deadline on every day, including the stress days of the first week of April 2026. IRB PDs in the CRS were at most one month old at every weekly DRC run, and the RFET counts were refreshed within ten business days after each quarter end. All timeliness rules are green.

documents.title: Change memorandum CHG-13-2025-01 – CRR3 IMA migration

sections.heading: Change description and rationale
sections.text: Change CHG-13-2025-01 migrates the Bank's internal model for market risk from the value-at-risk and stressed value-at-risk model approved under Article 363 CRR (version 2.4) to the expected shortfall model under the alternative internal model approach (version 3.0), to meet the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2024/1623 for the IMA. The change was recorded in the change log of the model inventory on 16 June 2025, when the model identification questionnaire for version 3.0 was confirmed and gate G0 was passed, before development started and long before any production use. The change introduces the ES with liquidity horizons, stressed calibration with a reduced set of risk factors, the SSRM for non-modellable risk factors, the DRC, desk-level back-testing and the PLA test.

sections.heading: Internal materiality classification
sections.text: The change is classified by internal materiality and, as the model requires supervisory permission, by regulatory class. It is internally material because it alters the methodology (ES instead of VaR and stressed VaR), introduces new material inputs (real price observations and a third-party observation vendor) and exceeds the output impact threshold of 5%. It is therefore subject to validation before implementation, passes gates G1 to G4 and requires approval by the Model Risk Committee as the approval authority for Tier 1 models.

sections.heading: Quantitative impact
sections.text: The impact was calculated on the same reference date, 31 December 2026, before and after the change: the own funds requirement for market risk of the IMA desks increases from EUR 214.0 million to EUR 235.7 million (+10.1%), and the risk-weighted exposure amount from EUR 2,675 million to EUR 2,946 million, which is +0.38% of the Bank's total risk-weighted exposure amount of EUR 71.2 billion. The impact on the model output is above the 10% threshold at the level of the range of application, and no desk changes its classification between IMA and standardised approach as a result of the change. The first-quarter 2027 parallel run confirmed the order of magnitude (+10.3% at 31 March 2027). The planned grid extension of version 3.1 is estimated to reduce the D02 surcharge by EUR 4 to 5 million.

deficiencies.rationale: The RDS documentation sets out the proxy hierarchy, the beta floor of 1.0 and a quarterly track-record test, and on its face the proxies appear conservative. Model Validation re-estimated the stress-period ES of the 204 proxied single-name CDS curves with bond-implied issuer spreads that are available for 2008–2009 and found that the beta-scaled sub-index proxies understate the stressed ES of the 61 financial-sector names by 7% (stressed reduced-set ES of D04 −3.1%). The track-record test is run only on post-2012 data, in which both proxy and actual history exist, and therefore cannot show conservatism in the stress period.

mitigation.text: Recalibrate the proxy betas of financial-sector CDS names on bond-implied stress-period spreads and extend the track-record test to stress-period data where bond spreads exist. Until then, apply a beta floor of 1.25 to financial-sector proxies and record the change as a revision of EJ-13-05.

deficiencies.rationale: The HPL–RTPL analysis of D02 attributes 71% of the unexplained variance to the SABR grid and 18% to the missing €STR–EURIBOR basis beyond 30 years. The remediation plan (grid extension in version 3.1) addresses only the first structural difference; the long-dated basis is recorded but has no remediation owner or deadline.

mitigation.text: Add the long-dated €STR–EURIBOR basis to the PLA difference register remediation plan with owner and deadline, and include it in the scope of version 3.1 or justify its exclusion quantitatively.

deficiencies.rationale: The expert judgement log quantifies six of seven judgements. EJ-13-06 (scaling of short NMRF histories to the stress period) is classified as high because it is not quantified, but the log neither gives a qualitative impact assessment nor explains why quantification is not possible, although the SSRM could be recomputed without the volatility-ratio scaling.

mitigation.text: Quantify the effect of EJ-13-06 by recomputing the SSRM without the volatility-ratio scaling (floor at 1) or document a qualitative assessment with the reason quantification is not possible, before the MRC approval of version 3.0.

deficiencies.rationale: The RFET uses a third-party observation vendor whose use has been presented to, but not yet permitted by, the ECB. The documentation reports RFET and SSRM results with and without vendor data, but the capital impact in the change memorandum (EUR 235.7 million) assumes vendor data are permitted; without them the SSRM rises by EUR 11.6 million.

mitigation.text: Present the capital impact without vendor observations as the base case in the application package and the MRC approval request until the ECB has permitted the use of the vendor data.
